newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada March consumer prices rise 2.0 pct on year.
newsitem.headline: Canada March consumer prices rise 2.0 pct on year.

text.p: Canada's unadjusted March consumer price index rose 0.2 percent in the month and 2.0 percent in the year to 137.6, Statistics Canada said on Tuesday.
CONSUMER PRICES - Pct chg Mar Feb
Unadjusted ex food and energy mth/mth +0.4 +0.1
Unadjusted ex food and energy yr/yr +1.7 +1.5

A Reuters survey of economists had forecast the seasonally adjusted CPI to rise 0.1 percent on the month and the undadjusted CPI to rise 0.2 percent on the month. The survey also forecast a 2.0 percent year-over-year rise in the all- items and 1.5 percent rise in the core CPI.
The core CPI rise of 1.7 percent was well within the Bank of Canada's target inflation range of one to three percent.

Statistics Canada said the month-on-month 0.2 percent increase in the unadjusted CPI was linked mainly to rises in the cost of clothing and footwear, air travel, pacakaged travel tours, piped gas and cable services. Lower gasoline and fuel oil prices as well as reduced mortgage interest charges help offset these increases to a small extent, the agency said.
Food prices were flat on the month, while energy prices fell 0.6 percent in March compared to February.
Clothing and footwear showed their third consecutive monthly advance, rising 1.2 percent in March, partly because of higher costs faced by garment manufacturers, Statistics Canada said.
Air fares advanced by 8.9 percent in March, and quotations for package holiday tours rose by 9.3 percent, the agency said.

The year-over-year increase of 2.0 percent was traced to significant price increases for food, energy, purchasing and insuring vehicles, and post-secondary tuition, StatsCan said. The climb was partially offset by lower mortgage interest charges.

The agency said the slowdown in yearly inflation in March was largely due to lower annual rates of increase for gasoline and food purchased from stores. Energy costs rose 4.7 percent on the year, considerably less than the increases between October 1996 and February 1997. Food prices rose 2.1 percent on the year.
